summary: Analyzes agreements between network providers for delivering quality of service across the whole Internet. It defines terms for inter-domain QoS and proposes the Meta-QoS-Class concept as a way to link providers' service classes while keeping the Internet as open as best-effort service. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Different delivery companies each have their own priority levels. This paper suggests a shared set of labels, so a rush package stays rushed across companies.

questions: how do internet providers agree on qos
subtitle: Linking network providers' QoS capabilities through common standards.

tldr.problem: Internet providers use different quality-of-service classes internally, but there is no standard way for providers to agree on QoS guarantees across provider boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes Meta-QoS-Class (MQC), a universal set of QoS performance targets that providers can publish and agree to support, replacing complex chain-based agreements between providers.
tldr.outcome: This allows providers to negotiate simple one-hop QoS agreements based on shared standards rather than complex multi-hop contracts, making inter-domain QoS feasible.

today: RFC 5160 remains an important framework document for inter-domain QoS thinking. It has not been obsoleted and continues to influence discussions of how to scale QoS across the Internet.

sections.title: The Problem: Connecting QoS Across Networks
sections.content:
Every large network provider manages its own quality-of-service (QoS) system inside its network using local classes and performance guarantees. The challenge is connecting these systems together so a customer gets consistent service quality from one provider across a chain of providers to reach a distant destination.

The RFC identifies three zones: single-provider networks (solved), multi-provider partnerships (manageable), and the global Internet (extremely difficult). This document focuses on the Internet-scale problem.
sections.eli5: Each company has its own priority system, but nobody has agreed on what those levels mean when traffic crosses between companies.

sections.title: Key Concepts: QoS Performance and Classes
sections.content:
The RFC defines QoS performance in three metrics: D (one-way delay), J (jitter, or delay variation), and L (packet loss rate). A local-QoS-Class (l-QC) represents one provider's QoS capability, described by (D, J, L) values.

When two adjacent providers agree to exchange traffic at a certain QoS level, they bind their respective l-QCs. An l-QC thread is the chain of bound classes across multiple providers.
sections.eli5: QoS is just three numbers: how fast, how shaky, and how much gets lost. Providers match their classes when they agree to work together.

sections.title: Why Simple Chains Don't Work
sections.content:
The intuitive approach is for one provider to guarantee QoS across an entire chain of providers to a distant destination. But this creates four critical problems:

First, agreements become destination-specific, so the number of agreements explodes with network size. Second, providers become liable for domains they do not control, creating impossible liability chains. Third, when one provider changes an agreement, it breaks all external agreements that depend on it (the SP chain trap). Fourth, this leads to glaciation: the network freezes because nobody can renegotiate anything.
sections.eli5: If you promise service through 10 other companies, you're responsible for their mistakes, and you cannot change your agreement without breaking everyone else's plans.

sections.title: The MQC Solution: One-Hop Agreements and Shared Standards
sections.content:
The RFC proposes that providers should guarantee QoS only across their own domain, not chains. This eliminates the chain trap and liability problems instantly. But to ensure consistency, all providers must understand the same QoS levels.

Meta-QoS-Class (MQC) is the answer: a global agreement on what specific QoS targets (D, J, L ranges) mean. For example, the "business VoIP" MQC might specify delay under 50 ms and loss under 0.1%. Providers certify that their local classes conform to published MQCs. Two l-QCs bind only if they both conform to the same MQC.

The Internet becomes a set of parallel MQC planes, each connecting all providers whose l-QCs conform to that MQC. A customer can pick the MQC plane best suited to their needs.
sections.eli5: Instead of complex multi-company promises, each company just says "I support this MQC" and connects with neighbors who support the same one.

sections.title: Routing and End-to-End Services
sections.content:
With MQC planes in place, routing within a plane uses standard BGP, one BGP instance per MQC. A BGP router can compute routes through available domains in the selected MQC plane, much like traditional routing.

The RFC notes that applications can request specific MQC planes and that QoS information (delay, loss) can be carried in BGP updates to help route selection. End-to-end QoS becomes a combination of choosing an MQC plane and selecting the best path within it.

The solution works incrementally: as soon as one provider joins an MQC plane, it can communicate with all other providers on that plane. Deployment pressure builds naturally without requiring global synchronization.
sections.eli5: Once providers agree on MQC standards, they use normal routing to find paths through any connected group supporting that standard. Services improve as more providers join.

sections.title: The Bigger Picture
sections.content:
The RFC is informational and presents a framework for thought rather than a protocol specification. Real implementation requires standardization of the MQC definitions themselves and conformance testing to verify that providers truly support the advertised classes.

The MQC concept relates to Diffserv (how to engineer networks) and service classes (what traffic requests) but differs in its focus on inter-domain federation. Because it remains agnostic to implementation technology, MQC can work with various routing protocols and QoS mechanisms.
sections.eli5: This paper explains the idea clearly but leaves the real technical details for future standards work.
